eyebrow: Python for Data Engineers · Chapter 8, Lesson 46
subtitle: Turning numeric location IDs into real, readable zone names.

eyebrow: groupBy() and agg() — real aggregations, at scale
code:
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, avg, count, round as spark_round

trips = spark.read.parquet("/data/nyc_taxi/yellow_tripdata_2024-01.parquet")

by_vendor = (
    trips.groupBy("VendorID")
    .agg(
        count("*").alias("trip_count"),
        spark_round(avg("fare_amount"), 2).alias("avg_fare"),
        spark_round(avg("trip_distance"), 2).alias("avg_distance"),
    )
)
by_vendor.show()
caption: Pandas' groupby().agg() from Lesson 24, now over millions of real trip records. alias() keeps column names clean and referenceable.
Each unique VendorID/passenger_count combination becomes its own group. orderBy() sorts after the aggregation runs.

eyebrow: Joining trips to the real zone lookup table
code:
zones = spark.read.csv("/data/nyc_taxi/taxi_zone_lookup.csv", header=True, inferSchema=True)

trips_with_zones = trips.join(
    zones, trips.PULocationID == zones.LocationID, "left"
).select(
    trips.VendorID, trips.fare_amount, trips.trip_distance,
    zones.Zone.alias("pickup_zone"), zones.Borough.alias("pickup_borough"),
)
caption: A raw PULocationID isn't useful in a report. The left join turns it into a real Zone and Borough name, keeping every trip.

eyebrow: A real aggregation after the join: average fare by zone
caption: Join first to get readable names, filter out bad fares, then aggregate — exactly the shape of the mini capstone's pipeline.
